title: NoOpPasswordEncoder in production code
risk: Passwords are stored and compared in clear text. Spring documents NoOpPasswordEncoder as not secure and kept for legacy and testing only.
fix: Use an adaptive encoder. PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder() encodes with bcrypt by default and supports password upgrades.
source: Spring Security 7.0 API reference: NoOpPasswordEncoder, PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder()

title: Authorization rule that can never be reached
risk: authorizeHttpRequests evaluates rules in order and the first match wins. A broader rule placed before a narrower one makes the narrower rule dead, so the access you meant to grant or restrict is not applied.
fix: Order rules from the most specific to the most general and end with anyRequest().
source: Spring Security 7.0 API reference: HttpSecurity.authorizeHttpRequests, 'Invalid Matcher Order Example'

title: Method security annotations without method security enabled
risk: @PreAuthorize and related annotations look protective, but Spring Boot's security starter does not activate method-level authorization by default, so they are ignored.
fix: Add @EnableMethodSecurity to a @Configuration class.
source: Spring Security 7.0 reference: Method Security

title: Deprecated @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity
risk: The annotation is deprecated in favor of @EnableMethodSecurity, which enables pre/post annotations by default and uses AuthorizationManager.
fix: Replace it with @EnableMethodSecurity.
source: Spring Security 7.0 reference: Migrating from @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity

title: CSRF protection disabled
risk: CSRF protection is on by default and should be disabled only when it makes sense for the application. With cookie or session based authentication, disabling it exposes state-changing requests to cross-site forgery.
fix: Keep the default. If the API is stateless and authenticates only with a token sent in a header, disabling CSRF can be reasonable: document that choice next to the call.
source: Spring Security 7.0 reference: Cross Site Request Forgery (CSRF), Disable CSRF Protection

title: Token authentication without an explicit stateless session policy
risk: The project looks like it authenticates with bearer tokens, but no SecurityFilterChain sets SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS. Depending on the setup, sessions may still be created, which does not match a token-based model.
fix: If the API is meant to be stateless, set sessionManagement(session -> session.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS)).
source: Spring Security 7.0 reference: Session Management, SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS (the token detection itself is a heuristic)

title: HMAC JWT signing key shorter than the algorithm minimum
risk: RFC 7518 requires an HMAC key at least as large as the hash output (256 bits for HS256, 384 for HS384, 512 for HS512). A key built from a short string literal is weak and easy to guess or brute-force, and some libraries refuse to use it.
fix: Generate a random key of at least the required size and load it from configuration or a secret store, not from a literal in the source.
source: RFC 7518 (JSON Web Algorithms) section 3.2, HMAC with SHA-2 Functions; Spring Security 7.0 reference: OAuth 2.0 Resource Server JWT, NimbusJwtDecoder.withSecretKey

title: Secret written as a literal in a configuration file
risk: Passwords, signing keys and tokens committed in application.properties or application.yml end up in version control, build artifacts and logs, and are shared by every environment that uses the file.
fix: Read the value from an environment variable or a secret store: key: ${ENV_NAME}. Keep dev-only defaults out of files that reach production, and rotate any secret that was committed.
source: Spring Boot reference: Externalized Configuration (property placeholders, binding from environment variables)

title: All actuator endpoints exposed over HTTP
risk: management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=* exposes every enabled actuator endpoint (for example env, beans, heapdump, loggers). Spring Boot exposes only health by default and says to make sure exposed endpoints hold no sensitive information or are secured.
fix: List only the endpoints you need (for example health,info) and secure the rest with Spring Security or a firewall.
source: Spring Boot reference: Actuator, Endpoints > Security and Exposing Endpoints (management.endpoints.web.exposure.include)

title: Stack traces always included in error responses
risk: Setting include-stacktrace to always returns the exception stack trace to every client, which leaks class names, library versions and internal paths.
fix: Keep the default (never) in production; use on_param only for local debugging, and log the stack trace on the server instead.
source: Spring Boot reference: Error Handling (server.error.* properties in Boot 3, spring.web.error.* in Boot 4); API: ErrorProperties.IncludeAttribute

title: Session or custom cookie without Secure or HttpOnly
risk: A cookie without HttpOnly can be read by JavaScript (stolen through XSS); a cookie without Secure can be sent over plain HTTP.
fix: Leave server.servlet.session.cookie.http-only and secure at true for the production profile, and set both flags on cookies you create.
source: Spring Boot application properties: server.servlet.session.cookie.http-only and server.servlet.session.cookie.secure; Spring Boot API: org.springframework.boot.web.server.Cookie

title: CORS allows any origin together with credentials
risk: Enabling credentials establishes a high level of trust with the configured origins and exposes user-specific data such as cookies and CSRF tokens. With a wildcard origin pattern, any site can make credentialed requests and read the response.
fix: List the exact origins you trust (setAllowedOrigins with explicit https:// origins) and keep allowCredentials only where cookies or HTTP authentication are really needed.
source: Spring Framework reference: Web MVC CORS, Credentialed Requests; Spring Security reference: CORS

title: CORS allows any origin
risk: A wildcard origin lets any website call the API from a browser. Without credentials the exposure is smaller, but Spring recommends a finite set of values for a higher level of security.
fix: Configure the specific origins of your front end, for example setAllowedOrigins(List.of("https://app.example.com")).
source: Spring Framework reference: Web MVC CORS, @CrossOrigin and Global Configuration

title: Every request is permitted without authentication
risk: anyRequest().permitAll() (or permitAll() on /**) turns authorization off for the whole chain. Spring Security documents anyRequest().authenticated() as the minimum rule for an HttpSecurity instance.
fix: End the rules with anyRequest().authenticated() (or denyAll()) and permit only the specific public paths such as /login.
source: Spring Security 7.0 reference: Authorize HttpServletRequests

title: Security response headers disabled
risk: Disabling frame options lets the application be framed by any origin (clickjacking); disabling headers removes the other default protections too.
fix: Keep the default headers; if one must change, adjust only that header (for example frameOptions sameOrigin for the H2 console in development).
source: Spring Security 7.0 API: HeadersConfigurer.FrameOptionsConfig.disable(), HttpSecurity.headers

title: JWT parsed without signature verification
risk: parseUnsecuredClaims, parseUnsecuredContent, parseClaimsJwt and parser().unsecured() accept a JWT with no signature check (alg none). If the token comes from a client and is used to authenticate or authorize, anyone can forge claims. Reading the claims of an already-validated expired token is a known legitimate use, so check what the token is used for.
fix: Parse client tokens with parseSignedClaims after verifyWith(key), or use Spring Security's JwtDecoder.
source: JJWT API reference: JwtParser (parseSignedClaims, parseUnsecuredClaims) and JwtParserBuilder.unsecured()

title: JWT created without an expiration claim
risk: A token without exp is valid until the signing key changes, so a leaked token stays usable indefinitely. JJWT provides expiration() for the registered exp claim.
fix: Set a short expiration on every token, for example .expiration(new Date(System.currentTimeMillis() + 15 * 60 * 1000)) for an access token, and validate it when parsing.
source: JJWT reference: JwtBuilder.expiration() and standard claims (RFC 7519 section 4.1.4)

title: Deprecated digest-based password encoder
risk: StandardPasswordEncoder, Md4PasswordEncoder, MessageDigestPasswordEncoder and LdapShaPasswordEncoder are deprecated: Spring documents digest-based password encoding as not secure and legacy-only.
fix: Use an adaptive one-way function (BCrypt, Pbkdf2, SCrypt, Argon2); DelegatingPasswordEncoder also supports password upgrades.
source: Spring Security 7.0 API reference: StandardPasswordEncoder, Md4PasswordEncoder, MessageDigestPasswordEncoder, LdapShaPasswordEncoder (Deprecated notes)

title: MD5 or SHA-1 digest in code that handles passwords
risk: Plain digests such as MD5 and SHA-1 are fast and unsalted by default, so stolen hashes are cracked quickly. Spring says digest-based password encoding is not considered secure. The scanner only checks whether the file mentions passwords, so the digest may be used for something else.
fix: If the digest protects passwords, replace it with an adaptive encoder (BCrypt, Pbkdf2, SCrypt, Argon2) through PasswordEncoder.
source: Spring Security 7.0 reference: Password Storage; API: MessageDigestPasswordEncoder (Deprecated note)

title: BCrypt strength below the default
risk: BCrypt is deliberately slow and Spring suggests tuning the strength so that verifying a password takes about 1 second. The default strength is 10; lower values make offline cracking cheaper.
fix: Use the default (new BCryptPasswordEncoder()) or tune upward on your own hardware.
source: Spring Security 7.0 reference: Password Storage, BCryptPasswordEncoder; API: BCryptPasswordEncoder (default strength 10)

title: Non-cryptographic random generator in secret-related code
risk: java.util.Random, Math.random and ThreadLocalRandom are not cryptographically secure, so tokens, codes or identifiers built from them can be predicted. The scanner only checks that the class path looks secret-related.
fix: Use java.security.SecureRandom (or a library key generator) for tokens, reset codes, one-time passwords and session identifiers.
source: Java SE API: java.util.Random (not cryptographically secure; use SecureRandom), java.security.SecureRandom
